text: Paper overview: George B. Field (1965) → Exhibit 01 / Field 1965 / Figure 2 How thermal conduction sets a small-scale limit. A fresh calculation of the condensation-mode growth rate in a uniform gas. Four curves connect Field’s linear theory to the scales on which structure can grow. Also explore Figure 3: the wave mode → Recomputed and numerically validated. This exhibit recomputes the published equation; it has not been compared point by point with digitized curves from the printed figure. The figure, recomputed. Field (1965), Figure 2, printed p. 540. α = 1/2, γ = 5/3; β = 0, 0.01, 0.1, 1. Both axes are dimensionless. Only the unstable branch and its neutral endpoints are drawn. Line styles and typography have been updated. SVG figurePNG figureCurve data / CSVValidation / JSON Physical interpretation Growth between two limits. Long wavelengths For this choice of α, the gas is stable to an isochoric perturbation but unstable to isobaric condensation. At small wavenumber, the finite sound speed limits the growth; the normalized rate tends to zero linearly with wavenumber. Short wavelengths Without conduction, the rate approaches 0.3. With conduction, temperature perturbations are smoothed on small scales. Each conducting curve reaches a finite cutoff beyond which the linear system is stable. From the paper to the calculation One cubic, one growing root. Field writes perturbations as exp(nt + i k·r): positive real n means growth. Using equations (27) and (38), define q = k/kρ, x = n/(kρc), α = kT/kρ, and β = kρ/kK. Here c is the adiabatic sound speed and the three characteristic wavenumbers are defined by equation (16). x³ + (α + βq²)x² + q²x + q²(α − 1 + βq²)/γ = 0 Equation (39), regrouped as a cubic in x. The heat-loss function is energy losses minus gains per unit mass per unit time. β = 0 is the zero-conductivity limit. These normalizations assume kρ > 0, as in Figure 2. For these parameters the polynomial is strictly increasing for nonnegative x. Within the unstable band it has exactly one positive root, which the code finds by bisection. At q = 0 it uses the limiting value x = 0. For β > 0, the neutral cutoff is qc = √[(1 − α)/β]: approximately 7.0711, 2.2361, and 0.7071 for β = 0.01, 0.1, and 1. The first lies just beyond the plotted range, as in the original figure. Stable-domain growth values are left blank in the CSV. Reproduce it Download. Run. Inspect. Save the three files below into one folder. Use Python 3.9 or later; the initial run used Python 3.9, NumPy 2.0.2, and Matplotlib 3.9.4. The calculation needs no source PDF, random seed, or external input data. reproduce.pyconfig.jsonrequirements.txtFull dependency versionsTechnical notes python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r requirements.txt .venv/bin/python reproduce.py --output output Outputs: PNG and SVG figures, sampled curve data, and a validation report. The report records parameters, package versions, and SHA-256 hashes of the code and configuration. Validation and limits Check the physics behind the curves. Compare the positive cubic root with eigenvalues of the independently assembled linearized fluid equations (11)–(14). Check the scaled residual of the cubic across four curves. Check the long-wave limit x/q → √[(1 − α)/(γα)] and the zero-conduction short-wave limit x → (1 − α)/γ = 0.3. Check the neutral root and the change from growth to damping across each conductive cutoff. All checks run before figures are written; failure stops the script. Measured errors and tolerances are in the validation report. The source equation, parameters, and overall curve shapes have been checked. A digitized comparison with the printed curves remains future work. This is a linear calculation in a uniform medium, without magnetic fields or gravity. Reported peaks are sampled maxima; the zero-conduction case has no finite-wavenumber peak. Source and next steps. George B. Field (1965), Thermal Instability, The Astrophysical Journal 142, 531–567.
